plain_text:
There's no single test for Parkinson's disease. Doctors usually
diagnose it based on medical history and a neurological
examination.
semantic_text: There's no single test for Parkinson's disease. Doctors usually diagnose it based on medical history and a neurological examination.

plain_text:
During the exam, the doctor will look for symptoms like
tremor, muscle stiffness, slow movements, and problems with
balance and walking. They may also do testing to rule out other
disorders with similar symptoms. These tests may include
blood and lab tests, as well as brain imaging scans.
semantic_text: During the exam, the doctor will look for symptoms like tremor, muscle stiffness, slow movements, and problems with balance and walking. They may also do testing to rule out other disorders with similar symptoms. These tests may include blood and lab tests, as well as brain imaging scans.

plain_text:
If symptoms improve after taking medication, this can
help confirm the diagnosis.
semantic_text: If symptoms improve after taking medication, this can help confirm the diagnosis.

plain_text:
There isn't a cure yet. But there are treatments available to
help relieve symptoms, especially in the earlier stages.
semantic_text: There isn't a cure yet. But there are treatments available to help relieve symptoms, especially in the earlier stages.

plain_text:
■ Medications. Levodopa is a common medication for PD.
It helps control motor symptoms by replenishing dopamine
levels in the brain. This medication is usually combined with
another medication to reduce side effects. Other medications
can help treat tremor, rigidity, and non-motor symptoms
like depression.
■ Deep brain stimulation (DBS). In severe cases where
medications aren't working well enough, doctors may
recommend DBS to ease symptoms. Electrodes implanted in
the brain send electrical pulses to the parts of the brain that
control movement. This can help reduce movement-related
symptoms and improve motor function.
■ Lifestyle and complementary therapies. A healthy diet,
exercise, and therapies like tai chi or dance can help manage
symptoms and improve overall well-being.
semantic_text: ■ Medications. Levodopa is a common medication for PD. It helps control motor symptoms by replenishing dopamine levels in the brain. This medication is usually combined with another medication to reduce side effects. Other medications can help treat tremor, rigidity, and non-motor symptoms like depression. ■ Deep brain stimulation (DBS). In severe cases where medications aren't working well enough, doctors may recommend DBS to ease symptoms. Electrodes implanted in the brain send electrical pulses to the parts of the brain that control movement. This can help reduce movement-related symptoms and improve motor function. ■ Lifestyle and complementary therapies. A healthy diet, exercise, and therapies like tai chi or dance can help manage symptoms and improve overall well-being.

plain_text:
Most treatments focus on improving the primary movement
symptoms. But some medications and therapies can also improve
problems with sleep, constipation, and cognition.
semantic_text: Most treatments focus on improving the primary movement symptoms. But some medications and therapies can also improve problems with sleep, constipation, and cognition.

plain_text:
Parkinson's disease is a chronic, progressive condition, and there is
no way to predict how quickly or severely the disease will develop
for any one person. While some people experience mild motor
disruptions, others become more severely disabled. But the good
news is that many people can live active and fulfilling lives for
many years after diagnosis.
semantic_text: Parkinson's disease is a chronic, progressive condition, and there is no way to predict how quickly or severely the disease will develop for any one person. While some people experience mild motor disruptions, others become more severely disabled. But the good news is that many people can live active and fulfilling lives for many years after diagnosis.

plain_text:
Between 500,000 and 1 million people in
the United States are estimated to be living with
Parkinson's disease (PD).
semantic_text: Between 500,000 and 1 million people in the United States are estimated to be living with Parkinson's disease (PD).

plain_text:
PD is more common in older adults as the risk
of developing it increases with age. The average age
of onset is around 70 years old.
semantic_text: PD is more common in older adults as the risk of developing it increases with age. The average age of onset is around 70 years old.

plain_text:
Although rare, some people develop PD as young as
age 50. This is known as “early onset” PD.
semantic_text: Although rare, some people develop PD as young as age 50. This is known as “early onset” PD.

plain_text: PD affects more men than women.
semantic_text: PD affects more men than women.

plain_text:
About 15% to 25% of people with PD have a
family member who also has the disease. Having
one or more close relative with PD increases your
risk of developing it.
semantic_text: About 15% to 25% of people with PD have a family member who also has the disease. Having one or more close relative with PD increases your risk of developing it.

plain_text:
SOURCE: NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF NEUROLOGICAL DISORDERS
AND STROKE
semantic_text: SOURCE: NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF NEUROLOGICAL DISORDERS AND STROKE

plain_text:
The National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke
(NINDS) supports PD research at NIH and across the country.
Current NINDS-funded research programs are studying how
the disease develops and progresses and are working to develop
new medications that can delay, prevent, or even reverse it.

plain_text: If you or a loved one is dealing with PD, you can:

plain_text:
■ Learn more about the research that's happening
■ Help with research and improve care for those with PD
by getting involved in a clinical trial
■ Find organizations that offer resources and support
